The brownfield-vendor trajectory is a legitimate, deliberately concrete instance, so keep the named product but ensure the role abstraction ('a dominant commercial identity-and-productivity suite whose authorisation lives in the provider's conditional-access engine') is what the reader is told carries forward.
rationale: This is a vendor-specific, not institution-specific, anchor. The whole section is explicitly framed as one of several trajectories ('For institutions whose authorisation logic resides primarily in...'), so the Microsoft naming is an illustrative scenario rather than a UL fact. It does not prevent institution-agnosticism, but a reviewer building a localization matrix should record that the brownfield-MS trajectory presupposes a specific commercial suite; flag low-priority parameterization only if the suite wants vendor-neutral trajectory labels.

surfaceForm: \gls{gdpr}~Art.~25 ... NIS2~Art.~21(2)(a) ... and (i) ... the EU AI Act ... Art.~5 ... Art.~50 ... 27001~A.5.15 ... NIST CSF PROTECT (PR.AA)
proposedGenericDecision: Role: 'the applicable data-protection regulation, NIS-equivalent directive, AI regulation, and ISMS/cybersecurity standards of the institution's jurisdiction'. The clause-level anchoring is EU-specific (GDPR/NIS2/EU AI Act) without naming a country, which implicitly binds the playbook to the EU regulatory regime. Parameterise the regulatory instruments so a non-EU adopter substitutes its own equivalents while preserving the by-design / access-control control intent.
rationale: Implicit jurisdiction binding: GDPR, NIS2 and the EU AI Act are EU instruments cited by article number with no country named, so the chapter silently assumes an EU-jurisdiction institution. ISO 27001 and NIST CSF are international/US and largely portable. To be institution-agnostic the EU-specific instruments should be expressed via a regulatory-mapping layer (\trchap{ch:regulatory-mapping}) keyed to the adopter's jurisdiction; the control objectives (by-design enforcement, access control) are universal and should be kept.

surfaceForm: the EU AI Act ... Art.~5 (prohibited practices) and Art.~50 (transparency) ... rules that gate AI-related TACs on context labelling and on prohibited-use classification
proposedGenericDecision: Role: 'the jurisdiction's AI regulation, including prohibited-use and transparency provisions'. The EU AI Act prohibited-practice/transparency hooks are EU-specific; express the policy-plane enforcement objective in regulation-neutral terms with the EU Act as the named instance.
rationale: The EU AI Act is named but the surrounding framing ('the locus where ... admit a policy-plane enforcement') treats EU AI-Act categories (prohibited practices, transparency) as the universal target. Non-EU adopters have different or absent AI regulation; parameterizing keeps the enforcement mechanism while letting the regulatory anchor vary by jurisdiction.
